title: What a Bad Book Teaches You About Reading Well
author: William Meller
summary: William Meller points to a curious tension in Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren's How to Read a Book: the method is built for great books, yet the authors' own pyramid says over 99 percent of books need only skimming. He argues that applying the full method once to a weak bestseller is still worthwhile, because the same rules double as a measuring instrument. Inspectional reading, the one-sentence statement of a book's unity and the effort to come to terms with the author's key words all expose weak books, whose chapters can be reordered like a pile of bricks and whose central terms shift meaning without warning. He stresses the brakes Adler builds in against the hasty reader, especially the rule forbidding agreement or disagreement before one can say I understand. Done in that order, a verdict such as this book is weak becomes a checkable critique. His conclusion is that one full pass on a book everyone praises calibrates the reader, after which the advice to skim first returns.
points: Adler's method works as a measuring instrument as well as a way to read good books, because weak books fail its tests of unity, structure and terms.
A good book has a floor plan in which parts serve a single unity, while a weak bestseller is a pile of bricks whose chapters can be rearranged without loss.
Two brakes guard against contempt for popular books: do not conclude a book is bad too quickly, and do not judge before you can honestly say I understand.
Following the full order of unity, parts, terms, propositions and arguments turns a vague opinion into a critique that others can check.
Apply the whole method to a praised bestseller only once to calibrate your judgment, then return to skimming first.
quotes: The whole book is a manual of analytical reading, which means asking questions of the text, finding the author’s terms, rebuilding the arguments, and only criticizing after understanding.

Calling a book a bestseller, then, says very little about it, for good or for bad. The list measures how many people bought it, and what the book is worth only shows up when someone reads it properly.

In a weak bestseller, the unity sentence usually comes out generic (the book “is about success,” “is about habits”) and the chapters accept almost any order without losing anything, which is a pretty clear symptom of a pile.
The method designed to climb up to the level of great authors also works as a detector when there is no level to climb.
The second is rule nine, the first of the rules of criticism, which forbids agreeing, disagreeing, or suspending judgment before you can say “I understand.

This book is weak” is an opinion. “This book switches the meaning of its main word halfway through and never proves what it promises in the first chapter” is already a critique someone else can check.
Whoever reads only classics never sees the ruler working in reverse, and ends up not knowing, precisely, why the good ones are good.
Once, with a book everyone is praising, is enough to calibrate.
